text.p: Two months before leaving power, the Nicaraguan government on Wednesday sent a proposed 1997 budget to the National Assembly for debate and accompanied it with a call for austerity by the next president.

Virtual President-elect Arnoldo Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance appears to have won the October 20 election, but apparent second-place finisher and former President Daniel Ortega of the left-wing Sandinsta Front has refused to concede. Official final results are due in mid-November.

Nicaraguan Finance Minister Emilio Pereira told a news conference the next administration, which assumes power January 10, must "not relax our current public spending policy, and must maintain our fiscal discipline" if the economy is to continue its streak of three consecutive years of growth.
The government has projected 5 percent growth in the gross domestic product for 1996.

The proposed budget forecast public spending of 5.555 billion cordobas ($634 million) against revenues of 4.031 billion cordobas ($461 million), producing a 1.524 billion cordoba ($176 million) budget deficit for Nicaragua in 1997.
The deficit will be financed through foreign aid and long-term, low interest loans from multilateral lending institutions, Pereira said.

Calling the free-market reforms implemented in Nicaragua in the 1990s after 10 years of Marxist Sandinista government "irresversible," Pereira said the next president must continue the economic program started by President Violeta Chamorro.

Nicaragua is fighting to pull itself out of an economic well brought on by years of civil war and failed economic experiments that has seen its standard of living fall to the levels it experienced in the 1940s.
When Chamorro took office in 1990, Nicaragua was wracked a collapsing economy, 15,000 percent inflation and the largest per capita debt burden in the world.

The tough, International Monetary Fund-sponsored economic reforms Chamorro introduced have reduced inflation and brought growth, but at the cost of jobs and reduced social spending to ease Nicaragua's brutal poverty.

"If we maintain an economic program that allows for eight percent growth per year for 15 consecutive years we will double our per capita income and raise it to the level we had in the 1970s," Pereira said.
